DomainKeys Identified Mail: Dein Mailser: DomainKeys Identified Mail: your mail server signs every email cryptographically. The receiver finds the public key in DNS at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>. The selector is just a name for the key, so several keys can exist side by side – for example one for your own server and one for a newsletter service.
Ein Dienst, der in deinem Auftrag sendet: A service sending on your behalf (newsletter, relay, ticket system) – recognised by its DKIM selector, for example.

Three records in your domain's DNS let receiving servers tell genuine emails from forged ones: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Large mail providers send you a daily report about the emails they saw in your name – this app collects and explains them.

„Passen“ heißt bei DMARC: Die von SPF od: In DMARC, "matching" means: the domain checked by SPF or DKIM must belong to the sender address. With relaxed alignment (adkim=r, aspf=r) the same organisational domain is enough, so email.example.org matches example.org. With strict alignment (adkim=s, aspf=s) the domains must be identical.
„Zugestellt“, „Quarantäne“ und „Abgewies: "Delivered", "Quarantined" and "Rejected" show what the receiver actually did. This can differ from your policy, for example when it recognises a forwarder as trustworthy – the report then lists an override.
